blocks.text: The classification of living organisms is organized into a hierarchical system that allows scientists to categorize and understand the relationships between different forms of life. This system includes several levels, known as taxa (singular: taxon), each representing a rank in the biological classification system. The primary levels of this hierarchy are: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, and species. Below is a detailed description of each level.

blocks.alt: Taxonomic hierarchy drawn as nine stacked, bell-shaped levels, each hanging from the one above and each with its label box: All Organisms at the top, then Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus and Species at the bottom. Colours run from purple at the top through blue and green to orange at the bottom.
blocks.caption: Figure 1.5: Taxonomic hierarchy (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 1.5).

blocks.text: It is the highest level of classification. Currently, there are three domains: Archaea, Bacteria, and Eukarya.
The kingdom is one of the highest taxonomic ranks, just below domain. It groups together all forms of life that share fundamental characteristics.

items: Example: In the domain Eukarya, there are several kingdoms, such as Animalia (animals), Plantae (plants), Fungi (fungi), and Protista (protists).

blocks.text: Phylum is the next level of classification below kingdom. Organisms within a phylum share a basic body plan and significant structural features.

items: Example: In the kingdom Animalia, the phylum Chordata includes all animals with a notochord, such as mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and fish.

blocks.text: Class further divides organisms within a phylum based on more specific common traits.

items: Example: Within the phylum Chordata, the class Mammalia includes all mammals, which are characterized by having hair and mammary glands.

blocks.text: Order categorizes organisms within a class based on additional shared characteristics and evolutionary history.

items: Example: Within the class Mammalia, the order Primates includes humans, monkeys, and apes, characterized by their large brains and opposable thumbs.

blocks.text: Family groups organisms within an order that are even more closely related, sharing more precise common attributes.

items: Example: Within the order Primates, the family Hominidae includes great apes and humans.

blocks.text: Genus is a more specific rank within a family, grouping species that are very closely related and often visually similar.

items: Example: Within the family Hominidae, the genus Homo includes humans and our closest extinct relatives.

blocks.text: Species is the most specific level of classification, representing a single type of organism. Members of a species can interbreed and produce fertile offspring.

items: Example: Within the genus Homo, the species Homo sapiens refers to modern humans.
